Abstract: This chapter evaluates the most recent grid codes for wind integration and highlights the need of both positive and negative sequence reactive current as a challenge. The chapter investigates two injection strategies: positive‐sequence injection low‐voltage ride‐through (PSI‐LVRT) and mixed‐sequence injection low‐voltage ride‐through (MSI‐LVRT) (i.e. PSI and NSI simultaneously), first with the conventional control and later with an improved control structure. Abstract: This chapters presents the operation and control of star‐channel MMC, building upon the passive (PC‐MMC) and active (AC‐MMC) cross‐connected modular multilevel converters used to overcome the technical issues in the conventional modular multilevel converter (MMC) during low or zero‐frequency operation. The conventional modular multilevel converter is modified into a star‐channel modular multilevel converter by interconnecting the converter legs using additional submodules in star configuration. The star‐channel provides a path for high‐frequency current components owing in the system and helps to minimize the capacitor voltage ripple during low‐frequency operation. The required number of submodules in the sub‐arms and star‐channels depends on the converter voltage rating. Generally, the star‐channel requires only 1 4 of the submodules in the main arms. In star‐channel MMC, each sub‐arm is equipped with an arm inductor, which mitigates the switching ripples and the inrush current. The star‐channel MMC requires twice the buffer inductors, but the equivalent (total) inductance remains same as that of the conventional MMC.

Abstract: This chapter replaces the cross‐connected capacitor with an active branch, named 'active cross‐connected modular multilevel converter (AC‐MMC)' to address the issue of capacitors voltage ripple. The new configuration of a modular multilevel converter is referred to as an active cross‐connected modular multilevel converter (AC‐MMC), in which the active submodules are connected across the mid‐point of the upper and lower arm of each leg. The active submodules are controlled to limit the current owing through the cross‐connected branch and provide a path for the power transfer between the upper and lower arm. The submodules in the upper and lower arm are controlled to generate the required AC output voltage waveform while maintaining the balance between the converter input and output power. On the other hand, the submodules in the cross‐connected arm are controlled to minimize the fluctuations in the arm power while maintaining the balance between the upper and lower arm powers.

Abstract: This chapter presents a new configuration of modular multilevel converters (MMCs) to deal with the submodule capacitors voltage ripple at low or zero frequency operation. The ripple in submodule capacitors voltage can be minimized by using either larger capacitors or by injecting a high‐frequency common‐mode voltage (CMV) and circulating currents into the system. The former approach is implemented at the design stage, requires large capacitors to minimize the voltage ripple, and increases the cost and physical size of an MMC. The new circuit configuration of a modular multilevel converter is referred to as a passive cross‐connected modular multilevel converter (PC‐MMC), in which a passive element is connected across the mid‐point of the upper and lower arm of each leg. The passive element is a simple capacitor, which provides a path for the power transfer between the upper and lower arms. Each converter leg is divided into two arms, and each arm consists of four half‐bridge (HB) submodules and two arm inductors. The half‐bridge submodule has a simple construction and requires one independent gating signal to control the devices.

Publication Title: Modular Multilevel Converters: Analysis, Control, and Applications
Abstract: This chapter deals with the implementation and performance of classical control methods for a modular multilevel converter. The submodule capacitor voltage control involves the leg voltage control and voltage balance among the arm submodules. The difference between the submodule capacitors voltage in the upper and lower arm of three converter legs leads to a circulating current. The circulating current increases the Root Mean Square (RMS) value of the arm current, resulting in an increase in the power loss and reduction of the system efficiency. The voltage balance strategy maintains the submodule capacitors voltage at an identical value within the arm. The voltage balancing can be achieved at either control stage using a closed‐loop controller or at modulation stage by using logical functions. The balancing method selects a certain number of submodules out of N submodules in an arm to generate the required voltage level. The operating voltage of modular multilevel converter can be increased by connecting more submodules in series in each arm. These submodules have floating capacitors, and their voltages must be controlled at their nominal value. The control of submodule capacitor voltage is a fundamental requirement to achieve a high performance current control, to improve output power quality, and to provide a stable and controllable operation.

Abstract: This chapter deals with state‐of‐the‐art and recent advancements in high‐power converter topologies. Voltage source converters (VSCs) have the highest market share and are widely used in industries. Several VSCs were developed in the past years. Among them, modular multilevel converter (MMC) is a highly regarded topology, which is the main focus of this book. The modular multilevel converter has several features such as modular construction, high reliability, and cost‐effectiveness because it uses low‐voltage, insulated gate bipolar transistor (LV‐IGBT) technology to reach high‐voltage (HV) operation. MMC is directly connected to medium‐voltage (MV) and high‐voltage (HV) grids without any step‐up transformer. A modular approach has been developed to overcome the limitations of semiconductor device ratings and their series connection to achieve higher operating voltage. The main features of matrix converters are sinusoidal input or output waveforms, a controllable input power factor, a wide range of output voltage and frequency control, and light‐weight design unlike that of cyclo‐converter (CCV).

Abstract: This chapter examines the role of modular multilevel converters in the power transmission systems and power quality improvement. High‐voltage direct current (HVDC) systems are the preferred choice over a high‐voltage AC (HVAC) transmission system for the long distance power transmission. The MMCs can be used as a series and shunt compensator to compensate the reactive power and grid unbalance in the case of power quality improvement. The static synchronous compensator (STATCOM) and unified power quality conditioner (UPQC) are the most popular power quality improvement devices. There are several MMC‐HVDC configurations such as monopolar and bipolar systems in the symmetrical and asymmetrical layouts are available to realize the two‐terminal and multi‐terminal HVDC system. The two‐terminal MMC‐based HVDC system is also referred to as a symmetrical monopolar MMC‐based HVDC system. The symmetrical monopolar configuration has one converter at the sending‐end and one converter at the receiving‐end station.

Abstract: This chapter discusses how the predictive control often referred to as a model predictive control approach is becoming more popular and is widely employed to control the power converters. The cost function consists of multiple control objectives, which are optimized for weighting factors to reach the desired system behavior. The resulting switching state is then applied to the converter. The digital implementation of model predictive control (MPC) approach requires a discrete‐time model of the MMC system. The discrete‐time (DT) model is obtained from the discretization of continuous‐time (CT) model. The front‐end rectifier of MMC is modeled as a constant DC source. The rectifier output is connected to the positive and negative bars of each leg of an MMC system through a DC‐line. The DC‐line is modeled as an inductor and a series resistance. The output current flows through the converter legs to the load. The difference between the upper and lower arm current gives the magnitude of the current owing through the load. The circulating current flows among the converter legs due to the difference between the upper and lower arm voltages. The circulating current mainly consists of even‐order harmonic components corresponding to the multiples of twice the fundamental frequency.

Abstract: This chapter discusses the possible system configurations of modular multi‐level converter (MMC)‐based motor drive systems and their control schemes. The transmission line and transformer leakage inductances act as a grid filter, which minimizes the switching frequency harmonics and improves the quality of the grid currents. The high‐frequency voltage component appears in the form of a common‐mode voltage (CMV) across motor neutral terminals and increases the peak value of motor common‐mode voltage. To block the common‐mode voltage, a simple transformer is added in the AC‐DC conversion stage. The DC‐bus voltage of motor‐side MMC is maintained at the rated value using the grid‐side MMC. The total DC‐bus voltage is equally distributed between the submodules in each arm of motor‐side MMC. These submodules are controlled to generate AC voltage with the required magnitude and frequency at the motor terminals, corresponding to the speed or torque and flux.

Abstract: This chapter provides some guidelines for modeling and simulation of the complex dynamics of the modular multilevel converter (MMC). Abstract: The parameter optimization for single-phase quasi-Z-source inverters (qZSI) is still an open topic owing to its superior advantages and widespread applications. Abstract:
Summary

Based on its unique properties, SiC offers unparalleled opportunities for industrial electronics in many medium‐ and high‐power applications. However, the still much higher cost of SiC devices does not justify a simple one‐to‐one replacement of other, mainly silicon components, but requires substantial system advantages to be realised. Key features of SiC devices are their low conduction losses, their low switching losses, and to some extent also their higher temperature capability. Especially mobile applications can benefit from the smaller size, the lower weight, and the higher efficiency of SiC electronics, by extending the range or reducing the storage. Applications, in which the frequency is a free parameter, can profit particularly from raising the frequency at bearable switching losses and, thus, reducing the size of passive components. In any case, an overall system optimisation is required to fully exploit the advantages of SiC and to prevail over the strong competition by other solutions based on silicon and increasingly also based on GaN. In fact, only very few SiC applications would be unfeasible without the advantages of SiC devices and, in some cases, even a mixed solution might be the optimum. In general, the large recent investments into SiC technology lead to price erosion of SiC components and open new application ranges for SiC – which increase the market volume even further and drive the economy of scale.

Abstract: The Smart Grid represents an unprecedented opportunity to move the energy industry into a new era of reliability, availability, and efficiency that will contribute to our economic and environmental health. A smarter grid will add resiliency to our electric power system and make it better prepared to address emergencies such as severe storms, earthquakes, large solar flares, and terrorist attacks. Because of its two-way interactive capacity, the Smart Grid will allow for automatic rerouting when equipment fails or outages occur. This will minimize outages and minimize the effects when they do happen. The new technologies will also help ensure that electricity recovery resumes quickly and strategically after an emergency—routing electricity to emergency services first, for example. In addition, the Smart Grid will take greater advantage of customer-owned power generators to produce power when it is not available from utilities. By combining these “distributed generation” resources, a community could keep its health center, police department, traffic lights, phone system, and grocery stores operating during emergencies. In addition, the Smart Grid is a way to address an aging energy infrastructure that needs to be upgraded or replaced. This book shows that Smart Grids can address energy efficiency, to bring increased awareness to consumers about the connection between electricity use and the environment, bring increased national security to our energy system—drawing on greater amounts of home-grown electricity that is more resistant to natural disasters and attack.

Publication Title: Smart and Power Grid Systems – Design Challenges and Paradigms
Abstract: The Smart Grid represents an unprecedented opportunity to move the energy industry into a new era of reliability, availability, and efficiency that will contribute to our economic and environmental health. During the transition period, it will be critical to carry out testing, technology improvements, consumer education, development of standards and regulations, and information sharing between projects to ensure that the benefits we envision from the Smart Grid become a reality. Today, an electricity disruption such as a blackout can have a domino effect—a series of failures that can affect banking, communications, traffic, and security. This is a particular threat in the winter, when homeowners can be left without heat. A smarter grid will add resiliency to our electric power system and make it better prepared to address emergencies such as severe storms, earthquakes, large solar flares, and terrorist attacks. Because of its two-way interactive capacity, the Smart Grid will allow for automatic rerouting when equipment fails or outages occur. This will minimize outages and minimize the effects when they do happen. When a power outage occurs, Smart Grid technologies will detect and isolate the outages, containing them before they become large-scale blackouts. The new technologies will also help ensure that electricity recovery resumes quickly and strategically after an emergency—routing electricity to emergency services first, for example. In addition, the Smart Grid will take greater advantage of customer-owned power generators to produce power when it is not available from utilities. By combining these “distributed generation” resources, a community could keep its health center, police department, traffic lights, phone system, and grocery stores operating during emergencies. In addition, the Smart Grid is a way to address an aging energy infrastructure that needs to be upgraded or replaced. This book shows that Smart Grids can address energy efficiency, to bring increased awareness to consumers about the connection between electricity use and the environment, bring increased national security to our energy system—drawing on greater amounts of home-grown electricity that is more resistant to natural disasters and attack.

Publication Title: 2D Nanomaterials: Synthesis, Properties, and Applications
Abstract:
Summary

In modern times, human lifestyle is heavily dependent on flexible electronic devices such as mobile phones, laptops, chargers, and electrical vehicles. One of the most pertinent requirements for these devices is an uninterruptible power supply. Currently, batteries and supercapacitors are the most widely used and researched electrochemical storage devices. Supercapacitors are preferred in applications that require rapid charge/discharge times. Other benefits of supercapacitors are their high‐power density, extended durability, and environmentally friendly nature. As electronics devices used on a daily basis require lightweight and high‐energy density energy storage systems, supercapacitors are preferred over batteries in these applications. Conventional supercapacitors suffer from the drawbacks of the requirement of an active electrode, the encapsulation requirement of the entire structure containing electrolyte and electrodes for prevention of leakage, and the rigid and bulky nature of the entire structure.

Supercapacitors with thinner and lighter technology incorporating flexible electrodes and electrolytic gel have been developed to overcome the above‐mentioned drawbacks. High integrity improved electrochemical performance, and rational design are some of the considerations for forming modern flexible supercapacitors. In addition, high performing in terms of electrochemical performance and thin and flexible electrodes, which can be bent, rolled, or twisted depending on the application, are essential requirements for modern flexible supercapacitors. For rapid and stable ion kinetics, the electrolytic gels should be mechanically flexible and highly conductive for ion movement. Thus, the development of highly flexible and simple materials is required for energy storage systems.

Owing to the presence of large electrochemical sites, graphene, carbon nanotubes, and transition metal oxides have attracted significant interest from researchers. Owing to the presence of multiple atomic layers, 2D nanomaterials have attracted tremendous interest for the manufacture of supercapacitor electrodes. The higher active surface area, mechanical integrity owing to the stacked layer, and controllable electrical properties are other advantages of 2D nanomaterials. Owing to their layered structure, supercapacitors based on 2D nanomaterials exhibit a fast electrochemical performance and fast ion kinetics. In this chapter, the applications of supercapacitors in electrical technology (microgrids), their controllers, and developments in supercapacitor technology for the application of 2D nanomaterials in them are presented.
IEEE Terms: Supercapacitors;Electrodes;Energy storage;Batteries;Nanomaterials;Electrolytes;Capacitors

Abstract: The book discusses the activities involved in developing an Enterprise Continuity Program (ECP) that will cover both Business Continuity Management (BCM) as well as Disaster Recovery Management (DRM). The creation of quantitative metrics for BCM are discussed as well as several models and methods that correspond to the goals and objectives of the International Standards Organisation (ISO) Technical Committee ISO/TC 292 “Security and resilience”. Significantly, the book contains the results of not only qualitative, but also quantitative, measures of Cyber Resilience which for the first time regulates organizations’ activities on protecting their critical information infrastructure. The book discusses the recommendations of the ISO 22301: 2019 standard “Security and resilience — Business continuity management systems — Requirements” for improving the BCM of organizations based on the well-known “Plan-Do-Check-Act” (PDCA) model. It also discusses the recommendations of the following ISO management systems standards that are widely used to support BCM. The ISO 9001 standard “Quality Management Systems”; ISO 14001 “Environmental Management Systems”; ISO 31000 “Risk Management”, ISO/IEC 20000-1 “Information Technology - Service Management”, ISO/IEC 27001 “Information Management security systems”, ISO 28000 “Specification for security management systems for the supply chain”, ASIS ORM.1-2017, NIST SP800-34, NFPA 1600: 2019, COBIT 2019, RESILIA, ITIL V4 and MOF 4.0, etc. The book expands on the best practices of the British Business Continuity Institute’s Good Practice Guidelines (2018 Edition), along with guidance from the Disaster Recovery Institute’s Professional Practices for Business Continuity Management (2017 Edition). Possible methods of conducting ECP projects in the field of BCM are considered in detail. Based on the practical experience of the author there are examples of Risk Assessment (RA) and Business Impact Analysis (BIA), examples of Business Continuity Plans (BCP) & Disaster Recovery Plans (DRP) and relevant BCP & DRP testing plans. This book will be useful to Chief Information Security Officers, internal and external Certified Information Systems Auditors, senior managers within companies who are responsible for ensuring business continuity and cyber stability, as well as teachers and students of MBA’s, CIO and CSO programs.

Abstract: When performing transient simulation in power systems using the time domain method, the mathematical model involves high‐dimensional nonlinear differential equations and large‐scale nonlinear algebraic equations (DAEs). This chapter discusses the operation phases in the semiconductor solid‐state absorber. The semiclassical treatment of semiconductor transport assumes the free Newton flights of carriers between instantaneous scattering events. There exist five major scattering mechanisms in semiconductor materials. The chapter details these five mechanisms. One can distinguish arguably between two types of semiconductor modeling packages as follows: software packages that model physics of semiconductor materials and packages modeling electronic behavior of semiconductor device. The chapter describes all three main types of blocking contacts that are fabricated at the front of radiation detectors depending on their applications. These are: the metal–semiconductor quasi‐Schottky junction; the metal–insulator junction; and the p–n junction. The chapter then focuses on the fabrication techniques of the ultrathin entrance windows in semiconductor radiation detectors. It also looks into the “dead” layer thickness, td, of the state‐of‐the‐art pn‐Silicon Drift Detectors.
